key_terms.meaning: A gas-charged vessel that stores pressurised fluid, smooths pump demand peaks and gives a short emergency supply after a pump failure.
F = p × A; on the rod side A is the annulus area
Hot compressed air tapped from an engine compressor stage and used for cabin air, pressurisation, anti-icing and engine starting.
p₁V₁ = p₂V₂ for a gas at constant temperature (absolute pressures)
A landing-gear strut filled with oil and nitrogen that absorbs landing impact and damps the rebound.
A switch on the landing gear that senses weight on wheels and inhibits gear retraction and some other functions on the ground.
E = ½mv²; the brakes take most of it as heat
The valve that meters fuel to the nozzles; on modern engines it is commanded by the FADEC computer.
A small turbine driven by bleed air that spins the engine through the accessory gearbox up to starting speed.
E = ½CV² for the exciter storage capacitor
The pressure altitude corresponding to the air pressure inside the cabin; transport aircraft normally hold it at or below 8000 ft.
A controlled valve in the pressure hull that lets cabin air escape; its opening sets the cabin pressure.
An air cycle machine whose turbine drives a compressor on the same shaft; the higher pressure gives a colder turbine outlet than a simple cycle.
An air cycle system with no compressor: the cooling turbine drives only a fan that pulls cooling air through the heat exchanger.
A safety valve that opens when cabin differential pressure exceeds its limit, so the hull is not overstressed.
A one-way valve that admits outside air when cabin pressure falls below ambient, so the hull is not pushed inward.
A valve that mixes hot bleed air with cooled air to hold the temperature selected on the cabin controller.
Δp = p<sub>cabin</sub> − p<sub>ambient</sub>; panel load F = Δp × A
A closed refrigeration loop that cools by evaporating a refrigerant at low pressure and condensing it at high pressure.
COP = Q<sub>evap</sub> ÷ W<sub>comp</sub>; Q<sub>cond</sub> = Q<sub>evap</sub> + W<sub>comp</sub>
A canister that releases oxygen from a chemical reaction when triggered, used to supply passengers after depressurisation.
V₁ = V<sub>w</sub> × (P<sub>c</sub> − P<sub>r</sub>) ÷ P₁
A fire detector made of two bonded metals that bend when heated and close a contact, warning of fire at that spot.
A tube run around a fire zone whose core resistance falls (Fenwal, Kidde) or whose gas pressure rises (pneumatic type) when any part of it is heated.
Junctions in the zone wired against cool reference junctions; a fast temperature rise gives a voltage that trips a relay (rate-of-rise detection).
V<sub>a</sub> = C × V<sub>z</sub> ÷ (1 − C); mass m = V<sub>a</sub> × ρ
A motor that shakes the control column as a stall warning when angle of attack approaches the stall angle.
V<sub>S</sub> = √(2W ÷ (ρ S C<sub>Lmax</sub>)); warning at least 5 kt or 5 % above it
Left and right flap positions disagree; the drive stops and wing-tip brakes lock the shafts
Keeping a surface above freezing so ice never forms on it, for example by ducting hot bleed air into a wing leading edge.
Removing ice after it forms, for example with pneumatic boots

takeaways: A hydraulic system is the muscle of the aircraft: F = pA at about 3000 psi, with two or three independent systems and normal, alternate and emergency modes.
An accumulator stores only a little usable fluid (Boyle’s law), enough for a few brake applications after the pumps stop.
One regulated bleed-air manifold feeds the packs, anti-ice and engine start, so a bleed fault touches many systems; stored-gas bottles give one-shot emergency power.
The oleo strut stores landing energy in nitrogen and turns the bounce into heat in the oil; brakes turn ½mv² into heat in the discs.
Fuel is metered by a unit the FADEC commands; oil cools and lubricates the bearings and carries debris to the chip detectors.
Starting ends well above self-sustaining speed; ignition is on before fuel, and a hot, hung or wet start is aborted by cutting fuel.
The outflow valve, not the supply, sets cabin pressure; the air cycle turbine cools the air by taking work out of it, and a vapour cycle moves heat with a refrigerant.
Oxygen keeps the oxygen partial pressure in the lungs up when the cabin is high, and must be on within the time of useful consciousness.
Fire detection must be fast, cover the whole zone and almost never cry wolf; each bottle discharge is one-shot, so engines carry two shots.
Gear, flap, stall and ice systems are electrical control and indication on hydraulic or electric drives: sensors, logic, lamps and warnings.
bank_note: Long answers on these systems are marked mostly on a labelled sketch plus the reason behind each part: why bleed air is precooled, why the outflow valve sets the cabin pressure, why fire detection must be fast yet free of false alarms. Most syllabi also ask for the electrical control and indication of landing gear, flaps, stall warning, ice protection and engine starting, so draw the system and name every part on the drawing.

bank.q: Draw a bootstrap air cycle cooling system and explain how it takes hot bleed air down to cold cabin supply air.
outline: Bleed air enters through a flow control valve and is cooled in a precooler
Primary heat exchanger rejects heat to ram air
Compressor raises pressure and temperature
Secondary heat exchanger rejects more heat
Turbine expands the air, doing work and dropping its temperature
Water separator removes condensed moisture before the cabin
Bootstrap: the turbine drives the compressor through a common shaft, so the air is cooled further than in a simple cycle
Advantages: colder outlet, better cooling performance per kg of bleed air
answer: Purpose: bleed air reaches the pack at about 200 °C and 2 to 3 bar, far too hot for the cabin. An air cycle pack uses the air itself as the working fluid: it removes heat to ram air, raises the pressure, and then expands the air through a turbine so that it gives up energy as shaft work and becomes cold.

svg.aria: Bootstrap air cycle pack: bleed air at 200 °C passes the flow control valve, the primary heat exchanger to 60 °C, the compressor to 120 °C, the secondary heat exchanger to 45 °C and the turbine to minus 37 °C, then the water separator and mixing with trim air before the cabin. A common shaft joins compressor and turbine; ram air cools both heat exchangers.

answer: Flow control valve: meters the bleed so the pack takes its design mass flow whatever the engine power, and shuts the pack off when commanded.
Primary heat exchanger: ram air from a scoop (or pulled by the pack fan on the ground) cools the bleed air at constant pressure, here from 200 °C to about 60 °C.
Compressor: raises the pressure of the cooled air. Its temperature rises too, but the higher pressure ratio across the turbine later gives a much larger temperature drop.
Secondary heat exchanger: removes the compression heat to ram air, bringing the air back near ram-air temperature but now at the higher pressure.

Turbine and water separator: the air expands through the turbine and does work on it, so its temperature falls well below 0 °C; the water that condenses is spun out in the separator (or removed before the turbine in a high-pressure water separation pack). Warm trim air is then mixed in to give the zone temperature the crew selected.

Ram air side: the ram air duct has an inlet flap that the pack controller opens and closes to set the cooling flow; on the ground, with no ram pressure, the fan on the machine’s shaft pulls air through both heat exchangers, which is why the turbine must give more work than the compressor takes.

High-pressure water separation: many modern packs put a condenser and a water extractor between the secondary heat exchanger and the turbine, with a reheater, so dry air enters the turbine. The turbine can then run below 0 °C without ice, and the pack can deliver colder air.

Temperature control: a pack temperature controller measures the air after the pack and moves a bypass (temperature control) valve that lets hot air round the turbine; zone trim valves add hot trim air for each cabin zone.

answer.text: Working with typical numbers (air, γ = 1.4, c<sub>p</sub> = 1.005 kJ/(kg·K), compressor and turbine efficiency 0.80; primary HX outlet 250 kPa and 60 °C; compressor pressure ratio 1.6; secondary HX outlet 390 kPa and 45 °C; turbine outlet 100 kPa):

answer: Bootstrap: the turbine drives the compressor on one shaft. The turbine gives 82.4 kJ/kg and the compressor takes 60.1 kJ/kg, so 22.3 kJ/kg is left to drive the fan that pulls ram air on the ground. In a simple cycle there is no compressor (the turbine drives only a fan), so the turbine works across the bleed pressure ratio alone and the outlet is warmer.

Advantages: light, no refrigerant, and the same air also pressurises and ventilates the cabin; it gives a colder outlet per kilogram of bleed than a simple cycle. The cost is the bleed air taken from the engines and poor performance on a hot stand.

Check: the air leaves at −37 °C, well below the 5 to 15 °C the cabin supply needs, which is why trim air is mixed back in; and the turbine work (82.4 kJ/kg) exceeds the compressor work (60.1 kJ/kg), as a bootstrap machine must for the shaft to keep turning.

bank.q: List the main components of an aircraft hydraulic system and state the function of each.
outline: Reservoir stores fluid and allows for expansion and thermal growth
Pump (engine-driven or electric) supplies pressure, typically 3000 psi in transport aircraft
Filters keep contamination below the specified class
Accumulator stores pressure and damps pulses
Pressure relief valve protects the system from overpressure
Selector valve directs flow to the chosen service
Servo valve meters flow in proportion to an electrical or mechanical command
Actuators convert fluid pressure into linear or rotary motion
Return line and heat exchanger close the loop
System controller selects pump, isolates faults and reports status
answer: A hydraulic system carries force from pumps to actuators through a confined fluid. By Pascal’s law the pressure is the same throughout, and each actuator gives F = p × A. A transport system runs at about 3000 psi (207 bar, 20.7 MPa).

answer.text: Components in the order the fluid meets them:

head: Component
Function
rows: Holds the fluid at low pressure, allows for thermal expansion and lets air separate; pressurised slightly so the pump inlet does not cavitate
Engine-driven variable-displacement pumps in flight; electric pumps for ground and backup; a hand pump or ram air turbine pump for emergency
On pressure and return lines; a bypass opens if one clogs, and a pop-out or switch warns
Nitrogen-charged store of fluid under pressure: covers peak flows, damps pump pulses, gives a short emergency supply
Opens at a set pressure and returns fluid to the reservoir, protecting the system
Directs fluid to one side of an actuator and connects the other side to return
Meters flow in proportion to a small electrical or mechanical command, for flight controls
Closes when the flow is far above normal, so a burst pipe cannot drain the system
Turn pressure into linear (jack) or rotary (motor) motion
Bring fluid back to the reservoir; a heat exchanger removes the heat of the losses
Selects pumps, unloads them at no demand, shows pressure, quantity and temperature

answer: Fluid: transports use a fire-resistant phosphate-ester fluid; light and many military aircraft use a red mineral-based fluid. They must not be mixed because the seals differ.
Architecture: two or three independent systems, each with its own reservoir and pumps, and a power transfer unit between two of them, so one failure cannot take every service.

Pumps: an engine-driven pump is usually a variable-displacement axial piston pump. A pressure compensator tilts its swash plate to reduce the stroke as pressure rises, so the pump delivers only the flow the users take and holds about 3000 psi. A case drain line carries its internal leakage, and a rising case drain flow warns of wear.

Open and closed centre: in an open-centre system the selector valves pass the pump flow straight back to the reservoir when no user is selected; in a closed-centre system, used on transports, the pressure is held at every selector valve and the pump unloads itself.
Monitoring: pressure, quantity and temperature are shown to the crew. A fall in quantity with normal pressure points to a leak; a fall in pressure with normal quantity points to a pump failure.

answer.text: Force from an actuator of piston diameter 5 cm and rod diameter 2 cm at 207 bar:
Accumulator store: gas volume 4.0 L, precharge 1000 psi, system 3000 psi, lowest useful pressure 1500 psi (Boyle’s law, constant temperature):
answer.pre:
gas at 3000 psi = 1000 × 4.0 ÷ 3000 = 1.333 L → fluid stored 2.667 L
gas at 1500 psi = 1000 × 4.0 ÷ 1500 = 2.667 L → fluid left 1.333 L
usable fluid = 2.667 − 1.333 = 1.333 L

answer: Check: pV for the accumulator gas is 4000 psi·L in all three states, and the retraction force is lower than the extension force by the rod area ratio, 1.649 ÷ 1.963 = 0.84, matching 34.1 ÷ 40.6 = 0.84.

bank.q: Explain the working principle of a typical engine bleed-air pneumatic system and name the services it supplies.
outline: Bleed taken from LP or HP compressor stage depending on engine speed
Check valve and pressure regulating valve hold manifold pressure
Precooler uses fan air to limit bleed temperature
Manifold distributes air; isolation valves separate left and right sides
Services: air conditioning and pressurisation, wing and engine anti-icing, engine starting, hydraulic reservoir pressurisation, water system pressurisation
Overpressure and overtemperature shut-off protect the ducting
Cross-bleed start allows one engine to start the other
answer: Principle: compressed air from an engine compressor, regulated in pressure and temperature, is the aircraft’s source of pneumatic power. Taking air the engine has already compressed saves carrying a separate compressor for each job.

Source selection: air is taken from a low-pressure (LP) stage at most powers. At low power the LP pressure is too low, so the HP valve opens and HP air feeds the system; a check valve stops HP air flowing back into the LP port. As power rises the HP valve closes.
Temperature: the precooler, a heat exchanger cooled by engine fan air through a fan-air valve, brings the bleed down to about 200 °C before it enters the wing and fuselage ducts.

Pressure: the pressure regulating and shut-off valve holds the downstream pressure to a design value of a few hundred kPa and closes fully on command or on a fault, under a bleed monitoring computer that reads duct pressure and temperature.

Distribution: the regulated air enters a manifold. Check valves let each source feed it but stop reverse flow; isolation (cross-bleed) valves split it into left, centre and right parts. The APU and a ground cart join downstream of the engine precooler and regulator, so they work with the engines stopped.

answer.text: Services supplied:

head: Service
What it uses the air for
rows: Cooled and expanded to supply and pressurise the cabin
Hot air keeps leading edges and inlet lips above 0 °C
Drives the air turbine starter; cross-bleed lets a running engine start the other
Stops hydraulic pump cavitation; delivers potable water
Door seals, cargo heat and trim air on some types

answer: Cross-bleed starting: with the isolation valves open, a running engine or the APU supplies the manifold of the engine being started, and its start valve passes the air to the air turbine starter. The engine being started must have its own bleed valve closed so the air goes to the starter and not back into its compressor.

Leak detection: loops of sensing element run alongside the hot ducts in the wing, pylon and fuselage. A leak of hot air heats the loop, and the bleed monitoring computer closes the valves feeding that section and shows the crew which one.
Indication: the crew sees duct pressure, valve positions and faults on the bleed panel or the electronic system display, and can select each bleed valve, the APU bleed and the cross-bleed valve.
Contrast: the bleedless 787 uses electric compressors for the cabin and keeps engine bleed only for the engine inlet anti-ice; it shows that the users, not the bleed air, are what the aircraft needs.

Protection: overpressure closes the regulating valve and a relief valve backs it up; overheat sensors and leak-detection loops along the ducts close the valves of the affected section and warn the crew.

answer.text: Duct check with the continuity equation: 0.30 kg/s at 250 kPa and 200 °C in a duct of 0.010 m²:

answer: Check: 1.84 × 0.010 × 16.3 = 0.300 kg/s, the mass flow we started with, and the density is about 1.5 times sea-level air density, as expected for air at 2.5 times sea-level pressure and 1.6 times the absolute temperature (2.5 ÷ 1.64 = 1.52).

bank.q: Why does an aircraft need cabin pressurisation, and how is cabin altitude controlled in normal operation?
outline: Above about 10 000 ft the partial pressure of oxygen falls and hypoxia sets in
Pressurisation keeps cabin altitude typically at or below 8000 ft
Conditioned air is fed in continuously and the outflow valve controls how much escapes
Cabin pressure controller schedules cabin altitude against aircraft altitude and limits the differential pressure
Differential pressure limited (about 8 to 9 psi in many transports) to protect the hull
Relief valves: positive pressure relief and negative pressure relief
Landing schedule brings the cabin to ambient before touchdown
answer: Oxygen: air is about 21 % oxygen at every height, but its partial pressure falls with the total pressure: about 21.3 kPa at sea level and 5.0 kPa at 35 000 ft (23.8 kPa ambient). Above about 10 000 ft the blood starts to load too little oxygen and hypoxia sets in: poor judgement, then loss of consciousness.

Time of useful consciousness, the time from losing oxygen to being unable to act usefully, falls from about 3 to 5 minutes at 25 000 ft to 30 to 60 s at 35 000 ft, so a cabin that stays at aircraft altitude is never acceptable on a jet.
Trapped gas: by Boyle’s law a litre of gas in the ears, sinuses or gut at 101.3 kPa becomes 101.3 ÷ 23.8 = 4.3 L at 35 000 ft, which causes pain and injury.
So the cabin is held at a cabin altitude, the standard-atmosphere height whose pressure equals the cabin pressure, normally at or below 8000 ft (75.3 kPa).

Control: the packs feed conditioned air at a steady mass flow. The outflow valve, a motor-driven gate at the rear, sets how much leaves; closing it raises cabin pressure and opening it lowers it. The supply only has to exceed leakage plus outflow.

answer.text: The cabin pressure controller follows a schedule:

head: Phase
Outflow valve and cabin
rows: Fully open; cabin at field pressure, no differential
Closes gradually; cabin climbs at a limited rate, a few hundred ft/min
Opens as needed so the cabin reaches field elevation at touchdown
Fully open, so the doors can be opened

answer: Controller modes: automatic, where the controller takes the planned cruise altitude and the landing field elevation and works out the schedule; a standby or semi-automatic mode where the crew sets a cabin altitude and rate; and manual, where the crew drives the outflow valve motor directly with a switch while watching the cabin altitude, rate and Δp.
Rate check: a cabin climbing to 8000 ft at 500 ft/min takes 8000 ÷ 500 = 16 minutes, which matches a normal airliner climb, so the cabin rate can stay within comfort limits.

Altitude limit: at a maximum Δp of 55 kPa the cabin can be held at 75.3 kPa only while the ambient pressure is at least 75.3 − 55 = 20.3 kPa; above that the cabin altitude must rise with the aircraft.

Limits: the hull is designed for a maximum differential pressure, about 55 to 60 kPa (8 to 9 psi) on airliners. A positive pressure relief valve opens outward above it; a negative pressure relief valve opens inward if outside pressure exceeds cabin pressure.

answer.text: Door load at 35 000 ft with the cabin at 8000 ft, door area 1.2 m²:

answer: Check: 51.5 kPa is below the 55 to 60 kPa hull limit, so the cabin can be held at 8000 ft at this height; the door carries about the weight of 6.3 tonnes (61 800 ÷ 9.81 = 6300 kg).

bank.q: State the requirements of an aircraft fire detection system and describe two detector types used in engine and cargo zones.
outline: Requirements: survive the environment, fast response, full zone coverage, low false alarms, fault indication, testable and resettable
Bimetallic spot detector: two bonded metals bend on heating and close a contact; simple and cheap; limited to spot coverage
Continuous loop: a tube or wire around the zone changes resistance when heated anywhere along it, giving full coverage
Thermocouple detector responds to rate of temperature rise rather than absolute temperature
Carbon monoxide detector used in cargo or cabin air to catch smouldering fires
Warning must reach the crew in the cockpit with a clear zone indication

answer.text: Requirements of a fire detection system:

head: Requirement
Why
rows: Signal within seconds, before a fire spreads
A false warning can cause an unnecessary engine shutdown or diversion, and teaches crews to doubt it
No shadow area where a fire could burn unseen
A broken loop or failed detector must show as FAULT, never as healthy
A cockpit test checks the whole circuit; the system resets without new parts
Vibration, heat, fuel, oil and cleaning fluids

answer: Engine and APU zones use continuous loops. In the resistance type an Inconel tube carries one centre wire (Fenwal) or two wires (Kidde) in a eutectic salt or thermistor core. Cold, the core insulates; hot, its resistance falls sharply anywhere along the length, and the control unit sees the drop and warns.

The pneumatic loop (Lindberg or Systron-Donner) is a sealed tube with a gas and a gas-charged core. An overall overheat raises the gas pressure; a local fire releases gas from the core; either closes a diaphragm switch. Both loop types give full coverage of a nacelle.

Cargo holds and lavatories use smoke detectors, because a fire in baggage smoulders before it flames. An optical detector shines light across a chamber; smoke scatters it onto a photocell. An ionisation detector loses current when smoke particles enter its ionised chamber.

Thermocouple systems detect the rate of temperature rise: active junctions in the zone are wired against cool reference junctions; a fast rise gives a voltage that trips a relay. A carbon monoxide detector can catch a smouldering fire with little smoke.

answer.text: Engine zones carry two loops, A and B, in AND logic. Working table of what the crew sees:

head: Loop A
Loop B
Indication
rows: normal (one loop alone is not trusted)
FAULT on A, and FIRE from B alone (single-loop mode)

answer: The control unit supplies the loops, applies a short confirmation delay to reject a transient, drives the warning light and bell, and stores a fault code. The cockpit test switch checks continuity and simulates a fire on each loop, so a broken wire is found before flight.
Flame detectors (ultraviolet or infrared) answer in under a second and suit some APU and military engine bays; they are paired or filtered so sunlight or a hot brake does not trip them.

False alarms come from dust, steam and condensation in cargo smoke detectors, and from chafed or wet connectors in loops; the design answers are the confirmation delay, AND logic between detectors and careful siting away from air outlets.
The warning reaches the cockpit as a red light naming the zone and a bell, and the zone light stays on until the fire is out.
Check: of the five loop states in the table only one, both loops faulted, leaves the zone unprotected, which is why a single broken wire never removes fire detection.

bank.q: An aircraft climbs from sea level to 12 500 m. Explain what the cabin pressure controller and outflow valve do during the climb and what the two relief valves protect against.
outline: Cabin altitude follows a schedule, not the aircraft altitude
Outflow valve closes as the aircraft climbs so less air escapes
Controller modulates the valve to hold the selected cabin rate of climb
Differential pressure rises and is limited to the structural maximum
Positive pressure relief valve opens if differential exceeds the limit
Negative pressure relief valve admits air if cabin pressure falls below ambient
Failure case: valve stuck open gives rapid depressurisation, stuck closed gives overpressure
answer: Data: 12 500 m is above 11 000 m, so the standard-atmosphere pressure is p = 22.63 × e<sup>−(12 500 − 11 000) × 9.807 ÷ (287 × 216.65)</sup> = 17.9 kPa. Take a hull limit of 59 kPa (about 8.6 psi) and a climb of 25 minutes.
On the ground the outflow valve is fully open and the cabin is at field pressure, 101.3 kPa at sea level, with no differential.
After lift-off the controller closes the valve a little so the cabin does not bump, then schedules the cabin altitude: it lets the cabin climb at a limited rate while the aircraft climbs much faster.

Pre-pressurisation: on many types the outflow valve closes slightly during the take-off run so the cabin is a few hundred feet below field elevation at lift-off; the change of pressure at rotation is then too small to feel.

Inputs the controller uses: cabin pressure from its own sensors, ambient static pressure from the air data computers, the planned cruise altitude and the landing field elevation, set by the crew or taken from the flight management system.

The controller modulates the valve continuously. It compares cabin pressure with its target and drives the valve motor: more closed to hold pressure up as the outside pressure falls, more open if the cabin rate is too low.

answer.text: Cabin schedule for a 25-minute climb at 500 m/min with the cabin rising at 300 ft/min (pressures from the standard atmosphere):

answer: So during the climb Δp grows from 0 to 58.8 kPa, just under the 59 kPa limit, and the cabin reaches 7500 ft, under the 8000 ft limit, at 300 ft/min, under the usual 500 ft/min comfort limit.

Positive pressure relief valve: a spring- or pneumatically-set valve that opens outward if the controller fails and Δp passes the limit, for example with the outflow valve jammed closed. It protects the hull from bursting.

Negative pressure relief valve: a flap that opens inward if outside pressure becomes higher than cabin pressure, for example in a fast descent with the valve shut, so the hull is not crushed by an outside load it was never designed for.

Failure cases: a valve stuck open lets the cabin climb fast (decompression, oxygen masks); stuck closed lets Δp rise to the safety valve setting, and the cabin must be depressurised manually before the doors are opened.
Check: if the cabin were held at 7500 ft (76.7 kPa) the limit would be reached at 76.7 − 59 = 17.7 kPa, a little above 12 500 m; so 12 500 m is about the highest this hull can fly with that cabin.

bank.q: One of three hydraulic systems fails in flight. Describe how the system controller reconfigures and which services are affected, using landing gear and brakes as examples.
outline: Each system has its own pump, reservoir and services; controllers isolate the failed system
Check valves stop fluid flowing back into the failed system
Accumulator gives a short reserve for one or two brake applications
Gear may need alternate extension (free fall or accumulator)
Brake and anti-skid may revert to a degraded mode or alternate source
Warning and status shown to crew so they know which services remain
Modes of operation: normal, alternate, emergency or manual reversion
answer: Architecture: a transport has three independent hydraulic systems (for example green, blue and yellow on the A320 family), each with its own reservoir, pumps, accumulator and list of services, and the flight controls are shared so that any one system can fly the aircraft.
Detection: the controller sees the failure as low pressure, low quantity or high temperature in one system, warns the crew and shows which services are lost.

Isolation: the failed system’s pumps are switched off, a power transfer unit that could pump its fluid overboard is inhibited if quantity is low, and check valves and priority valves stop the healthy systems feeding the leak.

answer.text: Reconfiguration of the services (a typical pattern; names differ by type):

head: Service
Normal supply
After the failure
rows: Remaining two systems; some spoilers lost
Alternate brakes from system 2, antiskid may be reduced
Lost or from a backup; steer with differential braking
One motor of the drive unit: flaps run at half speed

answer: Power transfer unit: if one engine-driven pump fails but its system’s fluid is intact, the PTU, a hydraulic motor and pump on one shaft, lets the pressure of a neighbouring system drive a pump in the failed one, so its services return without mixing the fluids.
Ram air turbine: if both engines or all main pumps are lost, the ram air turbine drops into the airflow and drives a pump (and on many types a generator) for flight controls and essential services.
Priority valves keep pressure for the flight controls first when demand is high, and hydraulic fuses close any line whose flow suggests a burst, so a leak downstream cannot empty the system.

answer.text: Brake reserve from the brake accumulator (4.0 L gas, 1000 psi precharge, charged to 3000 psi, useful down to 1500 psi; assume each full brake application uses 0.2 L):
answer.pre:
usable fluid = 2.667 − 1.333 = 1.333 L
applications = 1.333 ÷ 0.2 = 6.7, so about 6 full applications

answer: Modes of operation: normal (all pumps on their own systems), alternate (a backup pump, a PTU or another system for essential services), and emergency (accumulator, ram air turbine pump or hand pump for brakes, gear and a minimum of flight control).
Crew actions: follow the checklist, plan a longer landing distance, extend the gear by gravity early, and do not taxi far on accumulator brakes.

Why three systems: with one lost, the other two still power every flight control axis, and the loss of a second still leaves one; only the services that sit on the failed system alone, such as normal braking and gear retraction on many types, need their backup.
Check: about 6 full applications from 1.33 L is a short reserve, which is why the accumulator is an emergency source only and the alternate system takes over the brakes first.

bank.q: Describe the landing gear retraction sequence and the jobs of the uplock, downlock and squat switch, and explain how flap skew and asymmetry are detected.
outline: Squat sensor confirms weight off wheels before retraction is allowed
Sequence: doors open, downlocks released, legs retract into the uplocks, doors close
Uplock catches the leg and holds it against gravity and air loads
Downlock holds the side brace straight when extended; its sensors give the green lamps
Asymmetry: left and right wing-tip pick-offs compared; drive stopped and wing-tip brakes applied
Skew: neighbouring panels on one wing compared; drive stopped
Proximity sensors give position feedback to the cockpit indication
answer: Retraction is allowed only in the air. The squat (weight-on-wheels) sensor must show that the struts are extended, and the nose wheel must be centred, before the control unit accepts gear up.

answer.text: Retraction sequence:

head: Step
Action
Confirmed by
rows: Lever up; command to the gear control unit
Downlock actuators break the side-brace locks
Downlock sensors show unlocked; red lights
Retraction actuators swing the legs into the bays
Doors close; selector to neutral or pressure off
Door-closed and uplock sensors; lights out

answer: Uplock: a hook that catches a roller on the leg at the end of retraction and holds it against gravity and air load, so no hydraulic pressure is needed in flight. It is released first on extension.
Downlock: an over-centre lock on the side brace that holds the leg straight when extended, so the leg cannot fold at touchdown. Its sensors light the green lamps and feed the gear warning.
Squat switch: senses the compressed strut on the ground; it stops retraction even if the lever is moved, and switches many systems between ground and flight logic.

Flap asymmetry: position pick-offs at both wing tips report each wing’s flap angle; if the left and right angles differ by more than a small threshold the flap control computer stops the drive and applies the wing-tip brakes on the torque shafts.
Extension: lever down; doors open; uplocks release; the legs extend under pressure, gravity and air load; the side braces go over centre into the downlocks; the doors close and three greens show.

Alternate extension: if hydraulics are lost, a handle or switch opens the uplocks and doors mechanically or electrically and the gear falls under its own weight; assist springs push the braces into the downlocks.
Gear warning: a horn sounds if the gear is not down and locked with the throttles near idle at low height, and on many types when landing flap is set with the gear up; that one cannot be silenced.
Flap skew: sensors between neighbouring flap panels on the same wing detect one panel twisted or lagging after a track or actuator failure, and also stop the drive.
Indication: three green lamps for down and locked, red for in transit or disagreement with the lever, none when up and locked.

answer.text: Worked check with a strut: a main leg carrying 270.8 kN on a 0.20 m gas piston must have a static gas pressure of

answer: Check: a strut that shows extended in flight is at its full length with low gas pressure, which is exactly the state the squat sensor reads as "in air"; on the ground the 86.2 bar static load compresses it and inhibits retraction.

bank.q: Describe the engine start sequence from starter engagement to self-sustaining speed and explain the part played by the ignition system.
outline: Bleed air or electric power spins the starter through the accessory gearbox
N2 rises; fuel is admitted only above a minimum speed
Ignition is switched on before fuel so the mixture lights at once
Light-off raises exhaust gas temperature; the crew watch for a hot, hung or wet start
Past self-sustaining speed the starter cuts out (about 50 % N2 on one common engine) and the engine accelerates to idle
Ignition may be switched off after idle is stable, or left on in rain and icing
Wet start, hot start and hung start are the three abort cases
answer: Starter engagement: START is selected and the start valve opens (air turbine starter) or the starter contactor closes (electric starter). Bleed air from the APU, a running engine or a ground cart, or 28 V DC from the battery, turns the HP spool through the accessory gearbox.

Ignition: the exciter, fed with 28 V DC or 115 V AC, charges a storage capacitor to a few kilovolts; when it reaches the breakdown of a sealed gap the energy is dumped into the igniter plug as a spark, about once or twice a second. Two exciters and plugs give redundancy.

Electric start circuit (turboprops and APUs): the start switch energises a start relay whose heavy contacts connect 28 V DC to the starter-generator; a current limiter softens the first surge of several hundred amperes; a speed switch drops the relay at cut-out and the machine changes over to generating.
Interlocks: the start valve will not open with low bleed pressure, fuel is inhibited below the minimum N2, and the FADEC aborts the start by itself if EGT climbs too fast or N2 stops rising.

answer.text: Spark energy for a 4.0 µF capacitor at 2.0 kV:
answer.pre:
E = ½CV² = ½ × 4.0 × 10⁻⁶ × 2000² = 8.0 J per spark
at 1 spark/s: 8.0 W

answer: Igniters are energised before fuel: on one common narrow-body auto-start at about 16 % N2. Fuel is admitted at about 22 % N2, when there is enough airflow for a mixture that is not too rich, and it lights at once. EGT rises at light-off.

Starter and combustion together accelerate the spool past self-sustaining speed; at about 50 % N2 the start valve closes, the clutch overruns and the ignition switches off. The engine accelerates to idle on its own.

answer.text: Timeline with N2 rising at 1.6 %/s on the starter alone and 2.4 %/s after light-off:

answer: Ignition after the start: switched off at idle, or selected on continuously (low energy) in heavy rain, turbulence, icing and on contaminated runways so that a flameout relights at once.

Abort cases: a hot start (EGT passes the limit from too much fuel for the airflow), a hung start (light-off but N2 stops below idle), and a wet start (no light-off): cut the fuel and dry-motor to clear the engine.
Starters have duty-cycle limits: after a set cranking time they must cool before another attempt, because they are sized for a short job and would overheat if run continuously.
Check: the events come in the order 10.0 s, 13.75 s, 25.4 s, so the igniters are sparking 3.75 s before fuel arrives, which is the interlock the sequence is built around.

bank.q: Trace fuel from the tank to the combustor and oil from the bearing back to the tank, and explain how each system reports a fault to the cockpit.
outline: Fuel: tank, boost pump, LP pump, fuel-oil heat exchanger, LP filter, HP pump, metering unit under the FADEC, nozzles
Fuel cools the oil in the fuel-oil heat exchanger and works some engine actuators
Oil: pressure pump feeds bearings and gears, scavenge pumps return oil to the tank
Oil gives cooling and carries wear debris to the filter and chip detector
Sensors: fuel flow, fuel pressure, oil pressure and oil temperature
Faults shown as warning and status, with chip detection indicating bearing wear
answer: Fuel path: tank boost pumps (low pressure, stop vapour lock) → crossfeed and spar valves → engine LP pump → fuel-oil heat exchanger → LP filter with bypass → HP pump on the gearbox → fuel metering unit commanded by the FADEC → flow meter → HP shut-off valve → burner nozzles.

The fuel is also a coolant: in the fuel-oil heat exchanger it takes heat from the engine oil and melts ice crystals before the filter. On many engines fuel pressure also works the variable stator and bleed valve actuators.

Oil path (dry sump): oil tank → pressure pump → pressure filter → bearings and gearboxes through jets → scavenge pumps draw it from each bearing chamber → scavenge filter and chip detectors → fuel-oil or air-oil cooler → tank. A breather vents the air separated in the tank.

Tanks: vents keep the tanks near outside pressure; crossfeed valves let either engine draw from either side to keep the aircraft balanced; jettison pumps on some types dump fuel to bring the aircraft down to its landing weight.

The oil system has a relief valve to limit pump pressure and a bypass on each filter. The scavenge pumps have more capacity than the pressure pump, because the oil returning from the bearing chambers is mixed with air and must not be left to pool.
Oil jobs: lubrication, cooling of bearings and gears, and carrying wear debris to the filters and the magnetic chip detectors.

answer.text: Fault reporting to the cockpit:

head: Sensor
What it shows
Typical crew indication
rows: Filter clog caution before the bypass opens
Steel particles from bearing or gear wear
Chip caution (on some engines); found at inspection

answer.text: Numbers: 1200 kg/h of fuel of density 0.8 kg/L, and 0.5 kg/s of oil (c = 2.0 kJ/(kg·K)) taking 60 kW:

answer: FADEC inputs: thrust lever angle, N1 and N2, inlet and compressor pressures and temperatures, and EGT; it sets the fuel flow and protects against overspeed and over-temperature, and records fault codes for maintenance.

Typical faults and their causes: low oil pressure with rising temperature points to a pump or a blocked jet; a chip warning with steady pressure points to bearing wear; a filter clog with ice crystals in the fuel points to a fuel-oil heat exchanger problem.
Check: if the oil flow halves to 0.25 kg/s with the same 60 kW, ΔT doubles to 120 K, which is why falling oil pressure and rising oil temperature usually appear together.

bank.q: Evaluate the choice between hot bleed-air anti-icing and electro-thermal anti-icing, and say which you would choose for a high-bypass turbofan nacelle. Justify your answer.
outline: Anti-icing prevents ice; de-icing removes ice after it forms
Bleed air: uses hot air from the manifold, simple, proven, but costs engine power and raises fuel burn
Electro-thermal: pads or mats heat the skin electrically, no bleed penalty, but needs large electrical power and careful power management
Pneumatic boots de-ice by inflating to break the ice, used on turboprops
Chemical fluid systems give limited-duration protection
Choice justified with penalty on bleed extraction, engine efficiency and electrical load
Critical areas: wing leading edge, engine inlet lip, probes, windshield
answer: Definitions: anti-icing keeps a surface above 0 °C so ice never forms; de-icing lets ice form and then removes it. An engine nacelle inlet lip must be anti-iced, because ice shed from it goes straight into the fan and compressor.

answer.text: Comparison of the two anti-icing methods:

head: Point
Hot bleed air
Electro-thermal
rows: Compressor air of the same engine, ducted a short way to a piccolo tube in the lip
Generator power through cables, contactors and a controller
Bleed extraction raises fuel burn and EGT, worst at low power in descent
Shaft power for the generator; usually a smaller fuel penalty
Ducts, valves, regulator and overheat sensing; few moving parts
Heater mats, wiring, power control; large generator capacity
On-off or modulated valve; skin temperature limited by the bleed temperature
Fine zone control; can cycle de-icing zones to share power
Duct leak or valve stuck; overheat of the structure
Mat burn-out, open circuits, generator failure
Engine inlet lips on almost all turbofans, wing leading edges on most bleed aircraft

answer: Other methods for the full picture: pneumatic boots de-ice wing and tail leading edges on turboprops; fluid (weeping wing) systems give protection limited by the fluid carried.

Control and protection: a bleed anti-ice valve is opened by the crew or by an ice detector, a pressure regulator limits the duct pressure and an overheat sensor closes the valve if the lip structure gets too hot. An electric system needs a controller, temperature sensors in each mat and power switching for every zone.

Weight and installation: the bleed duct for a nacelle is short and simple; the electric option needs heater mats bonded into a curved lip, cables through the pylon and extra generator capacity, which all add weight and certification work.

Reliability: a bleed system fails mainly by a valve sticking or a duct leaking, which the overheat and leak loops catch; an electric system can lose a zone through a broken heater element, which leaves a cold spot that the crew cannot see.

answer.text: Estimate for a nacelle lip that needs 60 kW of heat in icing (assumed). With bleed entering at 200 °C and leaving the lip at 50 °C:
answer.pre:
ṁ = Q ÷ (c<sub>p</sub> ΔT) = 60 ÷ (1.005 × 150) = 0.40 kg/s of bleed air
electric option: I = P ÷ (√3 × V<sub>LL</sub>) = 60 000 ÷ (1.732 × 200) = 173 A per phase from a 115/200 V AC supply

answer: Evaluation: the nacelle sits next to the compressor, so bleed air needs only a short duct and no new generator capacity, and the lip can take the high temperature. An electric system would need about 173 A per phase per engine plus heavy wiring through the pylon, and a failure of the generator would remove the protection.
Choice: hot bleed-air anti-icing for the high-bypass turbofan nacelle. Even the bleedless 787 keeps bleed air for its engine inlets while it heats its wings electrically, which supports this choice.
Critical areas protected on the whole aircraft: wing and tail leading edges, engine inlets, air-data probes, windscreen and drain masts.

For a turboprop the answer changes: there is little bleed to spare and the propellers already need electric heat, so turboprops use pneumatic boots on the wing and tail and electric mats on the propellers, inlets and probes.

Running cost: bleed extraction raises specific fuel consumption only while anti-ice is selected, which is a small part of most flights; the electric option adds weight that is carried on every flight, so the fuel cost of the weight can exceed the bleed penalty.

Mixed design: many aircraft combine the two, with bleed for the engine inlets and the wing slats and electric heat for probes, windscreens and small areas, which is the arrangement most syllabi expect students to describe.

Check: 0.40 kg/s is a small fraction of the core flow of a large turbofan, while 60 kW of electric heat per engine is a large share of a typical 90 kVA generator, so the bleed option gives the smaller penalty for this one area.

bank.q: Analyse how stall warning and stall protection work together, and explain why warning must act before protection.
outline: Angle of attack vane measures local AoA and sends it to the stall computer
Stick shaker gives tactile warning at a margin before the stall angle
Stick pusher moves the column forward past a further threshold to force the nose down
Warning first gives the crew a chance to recover without automation taking control
Flap position, landing gear and Mach number adjust the thresholds (g stall and high speed stall)
Weight-on-wheels logic inhibits the pusher on the ground; both α channels must agree
Failure of one channel must be shown to the crew
answer: A stall depends on angle of attack α, not on speed alone: the wing stalls at its critical α at any speed. For level flight V<sub>S</sub> = √(2W ÷ (ρ S C<sub>Lmax</sub>)), and C<sub>Lmax</sub> depends on the flap setting.

Sensors: an α vane on each side of the fuselage turns a rotary transducer; the stall warning computer also takes flap and slat position and Mach number from the air data computer, because the stall α changes with both. Light aircraft use a leading-edge flapper switch or a reed horn.

Warning: near the stall α the computer drives the stick shaker, an electric motor with an unbalanced weight on the control column, with a horn or voice. Certification requires the warning to start at least 5 kt or 5 % above the stall speed, whichever is greater.

Protection: on types whose stall is hard to recover, such as many T-tail jets, a stick pusher pushes the column forward at a higher α. Fly-by-wire aircraft use alpha protection in the control laws and alpha floor, which commands full thrust.

answer.text: Numbers for an airliner of 64 000 kg and S = 122.6 m² at sea level:

answer: Mach number: at high Mach the stall α falls and the wing buffets earlier, so the computer lowers its threshold as Mach rises; at the other end, flap and slat extension raise C<sub>Lmax</sub> and change the α at which the stall comes.

Why T-tail jets need a pusher: at a high α the wake of a stalled wing can blanket a high tail, leaving too little pitch control to recover (a deep stall). The pusher stops α ever reaching that region.
Recovery the warning asks for: lower the nose to reduce α, level the wings, then add thrust; speed alone does not cure a stall.

Why warning comes before protection: the shaker gives the crew time to recover with a normal pitch-down and thrust, keeping them in control. A pusher overrides the pilot; acting first or wrongly it could dive the aircraft near the ground. So the pusher acts only at a higher α, after the warning has been ignored.
Safeguards: weight-on-wheels logic inhibits the pusher on the ground; both α channels must agree before it fires; the crew can cut it out; a channel failure is shown to the crew.

Check: the flap changes the stall speed by 145.1 − 106.2 = 38.9 kt, so a computer that ignored flap position would warn far too early with flap or far too late clean; that is why flap position is an input.

bank.q: Evaluate the design of fire protection for engine, APU, cargo and lavatory zones: why zone coverage and fault indication matter, and why each extinguisher discharge is one-shot.
outline: Detectors must cover the whole zone, because a fire in a corner must still be seen
Fast response limits damage; low false alarm rate stops unnecessary engine shutdowns
Fault indication in the detector loop itself must be shown or a failed loop looks healthy
Engine fire: two loops in AND logic, with automatic single-loop operation when one loop fails
A squib ruptures the bottle disc, so each bottle empties at once; two bottles give two shots on engines
Cargo smoke: detectors plus suppression; toilet: smoke detector and automatic bottle
After discharge the crew lands at the nearest suitable airport, because bottles cannot be recharged in flight
answer: Aim: detect a fire anywhere in a zone quickly, almost never give a false warning, and put enough agent into that zone to put it out.

Zone coverage: a nacelle has hot metal, airflow and many hidden corners, so a continuous loop runs around it and leaves no shadow; a spot detector would miss a fire a short way from its point. Cargo holds need smoke detectors spread across the ceiling because baggage smoulders first.

Fault indication: a detector loop that breaks or shorts must show FAULT, because a failed loop that looks healthy is worse than no loop. Dual loops in AND logic give both low false alarms (two loops must agree) and fault tolerance (a failed loop is dropped and the other works alone).

answer.text: Zone by zone:

head: Zone
Detection
Extinguishing
rows: Two bottles (two shots) through the fire handle or push-buttons
One bottle; automatic shutdown and discharge on the ground
High-rate discharge, then a metered flow until landing
Waste-bin bottle with a fusible link, fires by itself

answer: Why each discharge is one-shot: the agent is stored as a liquid under nitrogen pressure and released by a squib, a small explosive cartridge that ruptures a disc; the disc cannot be closed again, so the whole bottle empties in a second or two. A fast, full discharge reaches the design concentration before the airflow through the zone carries it away.

Agent choice: Halon 1301 breaks the chemical chain of combustion, so about 5 to 6 % by volume puts out a fire and leaves no residue on engines or baggage. It depletes ozone and is no longer made, so the industry uses recycled stock while replacement agents are certified.

Cargo classes: a Class C hold (the usual lower-deck hold) has smoke detection and a built-in system fired from the cockpit; a Class E hold on a freighter has detection, and the crew shuts off its airflow to starve the fire.

Because one discharge may not be enough, engines usually have two bottles, either one per engine with cross-feed or two per engine, so the crew can fire a second shot if the warning stays on (typically after about 30 s). Cargo holds use a high-rate bottle followed by metered bottles to keep the concentration up for the rest of the flight.

answer.text: Agent for a 40 m³ cargo hold at 6 % by volume, agent vapour density 6 kg/m³:

answer: Evaluation: the design trades weight against certainty. Bottles are heavy, so their number is kept small, while detection is duplicated because it is light; the result is a system where a single wire break or a single failed squib does not leave a zone unprotected.
After a discharge the crew lands at the nearest suitable airport: the bottles cannot be recharged in flight, and a cargo fire is only held down, not always put out.

Testing: the crew tests the loops and squib circuits before flight with a low current that proves continuity but cannot fire the squib; bottle pressure gauges or switches show a bottle that has leaked.

False-alarm cost: an engine fire warning leads to an engine shutdown and a diversion; a cargo smoke warning leads to a discharge and an urgent landing. Each false alarm costs money and trust, so the AND logic and delays are as much part of safety as fast detection.
Human side: the zone is named on the warning, the handle or button for that zone lights, and the checklist is short, so a crew under stress fires the right bottle into the right zone.
Check: the simple form C × V<sub>z</sub> would give 2.4 m³ and 14.4 kg, 0.9 kg less; a bottle sized that way would fall 6 % short of the design concentration.

glossary.def: A mineral or phosphate-ester based oil that carries pressure, lubricates moving parts and must not ignite easily.
A valve that opens at a set pressure to return fluid to the reservoir and so protect the system from overpressure.
A valve that positions its output in proportion to a small electrical or mechanical command signal.
The ducting that collects regulated bleed air from the engines and distributes it to the using systems.
A heat exchanger that cools hot engine bleed air with fan air before it enters the aircraft ducts.
The difference between cabin pressure and outside ambient pressure; the hull is sized for a fixed maximum.
The rate of change of cabin pressure, normally limited to a few hundred feet per minute for passenger comfort.
The seals in a hydraulic actuator that stop fluid leaking past the piston.
A system that releases brake pressure when a wheel starts to skid, so the tyre keeps grip and does not burst.
The gas and oil leg of a landing gear that carries static weight and absorbs landing and taxi loads.
A magnetic plug in the oil line that collects metal particles and warns of bearing or gear wear.
A pump that returns used oil from the bearings and gearbox back to the oil tank.
A plug that takes a high-energy pulse from the exciter and makes a spark in the combustor.
The engine speed above which combustion keeps the engine accelerating without help from the starter.
A compressor-turbine pair on one shaft that cools air by expanding it through the turbine.
A unit that removes condensed water from cooled air before it enters the cabin.
In a vapour cycle, a valve that drops the refrigerant pressure so it evaporates and absorbs heat.
The share of total gas pressure contributed by oxygen; the body needs a minimum value to stay conscious.
A crew mask regulator that opens on inhalation and mixes cabin air with oxygen, giving pure oxygen at high cabin altitude.
A hook on the landing gear that holds the retracted leg in place.
A mechanical lock that holds the landing gear extended and carries the load off the actuator.
Removing ice after it has formed, for example by inflating a pneumatic boot on the wing leading edge.
An actuator that moves the control column forward automatically to break a stall.
A small explosive cartridge that ruptures the disc of an extinguisher bottle when fired.
A hydraulic motor-pump pair that lets one system’s pressure drive a pump in another without mixing the fluids.
The ignition unit that charges a capacitor and dumps its energy into the igniter plug as a spark.
A sensor that detects a metal target without contact; it tells the gear control unit that a lock or door is in position.
The time from losing oxygen to being unable to act usefully; about 30 to 60 s at 35 000 ft.
